name: dynamic-range and video-dynamic-range
plain: Whether the screen can show HDR.
meaning: Tells a site to serve HDR video. Splits users into standard and HDR displays (modern iPhones, MacBook Pro, HDR monitors).

access.persistence: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored
access.iframe: Readable from cross-origin iframes too (same values)

limits.headline: Can check whether your screen can show HDR bright and dark detail
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the page loads.
can: Ask whether your screen supports high dynamic range
Serve HDR video or images if it does
Add the answer to a browser fingerprint
limits.reach_label: One yes or no, no prompt

story.what_it_is: Asks whether your screen can show high dynamic range, the very bright and very dark picture look called HDR.

marketing.name: dynamic-range media feature
marketing.pitch: Documents a media query that asks whether the screen and browser can show HDR content.

story.for_you: You never get asked. If your screen supports HDR, a video may look brighter with deeper shadows. If not, you get the normal version without noticing.
story.for_makers: Streaming sites avoid sending big HDR files to screens that cannot show them. That saves money. HDR also lets brands pitch a premium look.

use_cases.example: A streaming site sends HDR video only to screens that can show it, and plain video to the rest.
A cloud gaming site turns on HDR streaming for a supported laptop screen.
A photo or video editor in the browser enables an HDR preview when the screen supports it.
A brand uses an extra bright HDR ad on screens that can show it.
A TV or phone seller shows HDR product videos only to screens that can display them.
A team learns how many viewers can see HDR before paying to produce it.

legit_uses: Respect OS theme and accessibility needs
abuse: Infer disability or setting for fingerprinting
